interviewees.background: Serves as Senior Director of IT Infrastructure and Operations and describes himself as head of IT at his current company, overseeing infrastructure, applications, security and ITSM. His current company runs a custom ITSM platform that integrates with Microsoft Teams and uses AI to triage and create tickets; that decision was made by his predecessor, and the company had ServiceNow at one point. At his previous employer, Thermo Fisher, he was involved with a large ServiceNow environment covering Incident, Request, Problem, Change, Knowledge, CMDB, Asset Management, Major Incident Management, HR and a GRC rollout, moving off Zendesk. He described the evaluation against Jira, BMC, Zendesk and Workday's ticket management, the 9-12 month implementation, custom API integration work with Active Directory, Workday and Databricks, licensing and renewal terms, and the 3-5 admins who maintained the platform.

expert-1.label: Scalability was the deciding criterion
expert-1.statement: He ranks integration and scalability at the top of his purchasing criteria, and names scalability as the single factor that tipped the decision to ServiceNow: at ~2M tickets a year the prior system would break.

evidence.quote: I’d say the first is integration capabilities. At that scale, it has to work with your other systems. The second is scalability. Third would be cost, or total cost of ownership. Fourth, the user experience. And fifth, customization.
evidence.speaker: expert

evidence.quote: I’d say scalability. We were at a point where the volume of data and manual workflows in our previous system wasn’t scalable. When we left it, we were at around 2M tickets per year, and trying to do that on the previous system would just break it. So scalability was the top criterion—working with a Fortune 500 company at roughly $40B revenue and 2,000 sites—this was critical.
evidence.speaker: expert

evidence.quote: That's a good point—that once you're implementing something as big as this, it's very difficult to switch. However, I do like where the company is going, and I think ServiceNow met the scalability challenges we were facing. We got the integrations we needed, as well as the automated workflows. Overall, once we got it implemented, it worked well.
evidence.speaker: expert

expert-1.label: GxP/SOX compliance shaped the requirements
expert-1.statement: He repeatedly frames the platform decision in regulatory terms: a validated system, GxP-flagged change workflows routed to Quality, and compliance as something he would weigh above cost if a switch were proposed.

evidence.quote: Number one, the system was validated. For example, when you enter a change, you can check a box indicating it’s GxP-related. If it’s GxP-related, it triggers specific workflows for routing and the change process that Zendesk did not have.
evidence.speaker: expert

evidence.quote: Yes, it was about consolidating a lot of the IT tools—some of it was even paper-based. We wanted to improve service levels and MTTR and also be able to track our assets. In addition, we wanted better compliance—we’re subject to heavy regulations such as SOC, ISO, GxP, and SOC 2.
evidence.speaker: expert

evidence.quote: I would push back and question why that's the case. Cost might be one reason, but I would look at scalability, integration, and especially compliance from a regulatory perspective. We would look at things quite differently.
evidence.speaker: expert

expert-1.label: Internal validation effort is the hidden cost
expert-1.statement: He returns to the same overrun: the business-user testing and validation load was underestimated, adding roughly 20-30% in soft cost and stretching a 6-7 month plan to 9-12 months. He names it again as the main barrier to any future switch.

evidence.quote: The biggest pain points were lacking a clear definition of done—there was so much customization that scope boundaries were fuzzy—and underestimating the internal effort required. User testing wasn’t clearly defined, so we had to pull in resources who weren’t expecting it, and it was hard to secure their time.
evidence.speaker: expert

evidence.quote: In terms of expectations, the biggest miss was the internal level of effort and commitment—pulling additional resources for testing and validation. I’d say that added another 20-30% in cost. It’s soft cost, but we had to pull those resources away from other tasks.
evidence.speaker: expert

evidence.quote: The implementation effort, and the common underestimation of the resources required for validation.
evidence.speaker: expert

expert-1.label: Cost and complexity are the accepted tradeoff
expert-1.statement: He consistently describes ServiceNow as roughly double the cost of alternatives and complex to run and learn, while judging that capability, integration and scale justify it — rating TCO a 6 and still scoring 9 on continuation and recommendation.

evidence.quote: If we set ServiceNow at about $100 per user/month as a baseline, I’d put Zendesk at roughly $50-55. Jira was very inexpensive but lacked capabilities—around $20-21. So compared to Zendesk, ServiceNow was almost double.
evidence.speaker: expert

evidence.quote: It's expensive, especially for smaller companies. There can be a steep learning curve. Implementations are complex and require more internal resources than expected. For smaller teams, it can be overkill.
evidence.speaker: expert

evidence.quote: We have dedicated admins who maintain it, customize it, and create new flows, so there is ongoing work. You can also engage partners to help. There’s definitely maintenance and upkeep—probably more than other competitors because it can be a very complex system.
evidence.speaker: expert

expert-1.label: The custom ITSM left an asset management gap
expert-1.statement: He describes his current company's move to a simplified, AI-first custom ITSM as a decision made before he arrived that does not scale, and points to the missing IT asset management as a live pain point they may fix by buying back the ServiceNow asset module.

evidence.quote: One repercussion is we don’t really have asset management for all our IT assets, which is a big pain point for me right now. We’re now looking at possibly implementing just the ServiceNow asset management piece to categorize all our GMP equipment and IT assets.
evidence.speaker: expert

evidence.quote: I don’t think the decision was well thought through and it doesn’t scale, but for the company size at that time, I guess it made sense to simplify the user experience.
evidence.speaker: expert

evidence.quote: Yes. Yes, we're struggling now. We got rid of ServiceNow, and that left a gap in terms of asset management.
evidence.speaker: expert

expert-1.label: Integration was custom API work, not plug-and-play
expert-1.statement: Although he rates ServiceNow highest on integration, he stresses that in practice the connections to Active Directory, Workday, and legacy/Databricks data required a custom middle layer and direct APIs rather than out-of-the-box connectors.

evidence.quote: It integrated well, but it took time to build. We set up single sign-on with Active Directory and integrated Workday. It wasn’t plug-and-play; our engineers and identity access management team had to do quite a bit of work.
evidence.speaker: expert

evidence.quote: They had some out-of-the-box APIs, but we had legacy systems and tools that those APIs wouldn’t connect to, so we built a middle layer to make them talk. For example, we wanted to bring in Databricks data related to certain service tickets. There was a Databricks connector, but a lot of our legacy ERP data was feeding Databricks and the connector didn’t have access to it, so we wrote a custom API to integrate the two.
evidence.speaker: expert

evidence.quote: First, we’d want a live demo of the capabilities. From there, we might ask for customer references, but we’d start with a product demonstration to show they truly have the capabilities. Next, a short POC to prove it. For example, on integration, we’d ask, can you integrate with Workday? If they said yes in the demo, we’d say, show us.
evidence.speaker: expert

expert-1.label: AI capability is the competitive frontier
expert-1.statement: He cites AI as both the reason his current company chose an AI-first custom tool over ServiceNow and as what he admires about ServiceNow's direction now (agents, Moveworks), and names an AI story as part of what a competitor would need to pull him away.

evidence.quote: At the time, they weren’t leaning into it as heavily; the vendor we chose was taking an AI-first approach. That was the major difference. Since then, I think they’ve grown in their AI capabilities. Cost was also a factor—we saw lower licensing costs.
evidence.speaker: expert

evidence.quote: Definitely cost—lower implementation cost and leaning into AI. And if they could port the data from ServiceNow to one of those systems and reduce implementation time, that would be significant.
evidence.speaker: expert

evidence.quote: I'd say it has really powerful workflows and automation, and strong enterprise integrations and scalability. It's got strong modules to support ITSM and even areas like IT Operations and GRC, and now they're really leaning into AI.
evidence.speaker: expert

expert-1.label: Switching is hard, but not ERP-hard
expert-1.statement: He puts the difficulty of migrating off ServiceNow at 7-8 out of 10 versus 10 for an ERP, estimating $1M-$1.5M and at least a year, with performance failure or a 30-50% cost increase as the triggers that would make him look.

evidence.quote: Yes, it would. Switching would be very difficult. On a scale of 1 to 10, it's not as difficult as an ERP system—I'd put ERP at 10, a multi-million-dollar project that takes 2-3 years to switch. This would be around 7-8. You'd still make a significant investment, around $1M-$1.5M, and invest a lot of time—at least a year for implementation.
evidence.speaker: expert

evidence.quote: If there were significant performance issues. Also, a 30-50% cost increase—where it becomes unbearable—would be another reason to switch.
evidence.speaker: expert

expert-2.label: GxP compliance drove the platform decision

evidence.quote: We were also getting pressure from Quality and Regulatory to have better audit trails on changes, since a lot of our systems touch GxP-relevant processes. So it was really scalability, asset visibility, and compliance-grade change control.
evidence.speaker: expert

evidence.quote: BMC had more of that baked in already from working with other pharma and med device customers. So BMC gave us the best balance of cost and compliance readiness.
evidence.speaker: expert

evidence.quote: Probably Ivanti. They're close on cost and on general ITSM functionality. Where BMC pulled ahead was specifically in how much pre-built compliance content they had for regulated industries.

evidence.quote: First would be total cost of ownership. Second, out-of-the-box support for compliance workflows. Third, implementation speed. Fourth, integration capability. And fifth, ease of administration for a small team.

evidence.quote: ServiceNow was excellent but it was almost triple our BMC quote for a comparable module set, and for our size, that wasn't defensible internally.
